summary: Defines the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant for devices that lack a browser or are input constrained, such as smart TVs, media consoles, and printers. They can get user authorization via another device. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: On a TV with a hard-to-use keyboard, you see a short code, then approve it on your phone.

subtitle: How a TV or printer with no good keyboard gets your permission by showing a short code you approve on your phone.

tldr.problem: Smart TVs, media consoles, printers and similar devices lack a suitable browser or an easy way to type, so the usual browser-based OAuth redirect flows do not work for them.
tldr.mechanism: The device asks the authorization server for a device code and a short user code, shows the user code and a URI, and polls the token endpoint while the user approves on a second device such as a phone.
tldr.outcome: The device gets an access token after the user approves on another device. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8628 is a Proposed Standard from August 2019, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6749.

sections.title: The Problem and the Device Flow
sections.content:
RFC 8628 extends OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) for devices with limited input or no suitable browser, such as smart TVs, media consoles, picture frames and printers. The device flow asks the user to review the request on a secondary device, such as a smartphone, that has a browser and a decent input method.

It is not meant to replace browser-based OAuth in native apps on capable devices like smartphones; those should follow RFC 8252. The operating requirements are that the device is online, can make outbound HTTPS requests, can show or otherwise communicate a URI and code, and that the user has a secondary device.

Unlike the authorization code grant, the device does not need two-way communication with the user's browser. It cannot receive incoming requests, so it polls the authorization server until the user finishes.
sections.plainLanguage: A TV is bad at typing passwords, but your phone is good at it. So the TV shows a code and your phone does the approving.

sections.title: The Six Steps
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows six steps, labeled A to F.

  • A: the client sends its client identifier to the authorization server.
  • B: the server returns a device code, a user code and a verification URI.
  • C: the client tells the user to visit the URI on another device and enter the user code.
  • D: the server authenticates the user, asks for the user code, validates it and prompts the user to accept or decline.
  • E: meanwhile, the client repeatedly polls with the device code and its client identifier.
  • F: the server responds with an access token (and optionally a refresh token), an error, or an indication to keep polling.
sections.plainLanguage: The TV asks for a code, shows it to you, you type it on your phone and say yes. All the while the TV keeps asking 'did they say yes yet?'

sections.title: Device Authorization Request and Response
sections.content:
The client makes an HTTP POST to the new device authorization endpoint with client_id (required unless it authenticates as in RFC 6749) and an optional scope, in application/x-www-form-urlencoded format. All requests from the device MUST use TLS. To avoid overloading the token endpoint, the client SHOULD only start a request when prompted by the user, not automatically at app start.

The server replies with 200 OK and a JSON body: device_code, user_code and verification_uri (all required), an optional verification_uri_complete, expires_in (required, the lifetime in seconds of both codes) and an optional interval, the minimum seconds to wait between polls. If no interval is given, clients MUST use 5.

The verification URI should be short and easy to remember because the user types it. The device_code is not for the user and should not be displayed.
sections.plainLanguage: The TV asks the server for a pair of codes. One is long and secret for the TV, and one is short for you to type.

sections.title: User Interaction and Polling
sections.content:
The device shows the user_code and verification_uri. The user opens the URI in a browser on another device, authenticates over TLS, enters the code, and approves or denies the request. Beyond starting at the URI and supplying the code, the exact sequence is up to the server. If verification_uri_complete is provided, the client MAY show it as a QR code or via NFC, but it is RECOMMENDED to still show the text URI, and the client MUST still display the user code so the user can confirm they are authorizing the right device.

The client polls the token endpoint with a grant_type of urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code plus the device_code. Error codes steer the polling:

  • authorization_pending: keep polling, waiting at least the interval (or 5 seconds).
  • slow_down: keep polling, but the interval MUST grow by 5 seconds for this and all later requests.
  • access_denied: the user denied the request.
  • expired_token: the device code expired; the client MAY start over but SHOULD wait for user interaction first.

Any other error means stop polling. On a connection timeout, clients MUST reduce their polling frequency, and exponential backoff such as doubling the interval is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The TV asks 'yes yet?' every few seconds. If the server says 'slow down', the TV waits longer between questions. If it says 'no' or 'too late', the TV stops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because users type the user code, it is short and has less entropy than the device code, so the server is advised to rate-limit attempts. The RFC gives an example: an 8-character base 20 code (about 34.5 bits of entropy) would need a rate-limiting interval and validity period that allow only 5 attempts to reach a 2^-32 chance of a lucky guess. The device code is never typed, so a very high entropy code SHOULD be used.

The RFC also covers other risks.

  • Remote phishing: an attacker may email a victim the verification URL and a code. Servers should tell users they are authorizing a device, confirm it is in their possession, and show device information. Short code lifetimes limit codes sent by email.
  • Session spying: someone watching the screen could finish authorization first.
  • Non-confidential clients: device clients usually cannot keep credentials secret and should be treated as public clients.
  • Device trustworthiness: a malicious authorization server could mount a man-in-the-middle attack, though the user might notice the wrong URL.
sections.plainLanguage: A short code is easy to type but also easier to guess, so the server limits tries. You should only approve a code that is on a screen in front of you.

sections.title: User Codes, Discovery and Registrations
sections.content:
The usability section suggests a code made of case-insensitive letters with vowels removed, giving the base 20 set BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ. The example WDJB-MJHT has 8 significant characters, with a dash for readability. Numeric codes also work but need to be longer, for example 9 digits such as 019-450-730. Servers should strip dashes and punctuation when reading input, and uppercase letters before comparing. Character sets with easily confused characters like 0 and O are best avoided.

Support is declared in authorization server metadata (RFC 8414): the grant type URN goes in grant_types_supported, and a new optional key device_authorization_endpoint gives the endpoint URL. IANA registered the device_code parameter, the grant type URN, the four new error values and the metadata name.
sections.plainLanguage: Codes use letters that are easy to type on a phone and hard to mix up, and the dash is just so you can read it.
